name: Pie and Mash
description: A minced beef pie served with mashed potato and a green parsley sauce called liquor. It is the classic meal of London's traditional pie and mash shops, a working-class staple since the 19th century.
how_to_eat: Eat with a fork and spoon, with plenty of liquor poured over and malt vinegar or chilli vinegar to taste.
how_to_order: Order 'pie and mash with liquor' at an East End pie and mash shop.

name: Jellied Eels
description: Chopped eels boiled in a spiced stock that sets into a jelly as it cools, served cold. A traditional East End dish dating from the 18th century, often sold alongside pie and mash.
how_to_eat: Eat cold with a sprinkle of chilli vinegar and white pepper.
how_to_order: Ask for a pot of jellied eels at a pie and mash shop or an East End eel stall.

name: Fish and Chips
description: Battered fried fish, most commonly cod or haddock, served with chips. Often considered the national dish of the United Kingdom, it has been sold from fish-and-chip shops since the 1860s.
how_to_eat: Season with salt and malt vinegar and eat with mushy peas or tartare sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'cod and chips' or 'haddock and chips' at a fish and chip shop.

name: Full English Breakfast
description: A cooked breakfast of bacon, sausages, eggs, tomatoes, mushrooms and black pudding with toast or fried bread; baked beans are a common modern addition. It became popular in the Victorian era and is usually served with tea.
how_to_eat: Eat as a late, big breakfast with toast and a mug of tea.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'full English' at any café ('caff') or pub serving breakfast.

name: Sunday Roast
description: Roast meat with roast or mashed potatoes, vegetables and accompaniments such as Yorkshire pudding, gravy and stuffing. It is traditionally eaten on Sunday, originally after the church service.
how_to_eat: Pour gravy over everything; beef is traditionally paired with horseradish and Yorkshire pudding.
how_to_order: Order the Sunday roast at a pub on Sunday lunchtime; booking ahead helps.

name: Eton Mess
description: A dessert of strawberries, broken meringue and whipped cream mixed together. It is named after Eton College, where it is served at the annual cricket match against Harrow.
how_to_eat: Eat chilled from a glass or bowl in summer.
how_to_order: Look for it on summer dessert menus in pubs and restaurants.

name: Cornish Pasty
description: A D-shaped pastry with a crimped edge filled with beef, potato, swede and onion, lightly seasoned with salt and pepper. 'Cornish pasty' is a Protected Geographical Indication and must be made in Cornwall to that recipe.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, holding the crimped crust.
how_to_order: Buy one hot from a Cornish bakery or pasty shop.

name: Cream Tea
description: Scones served with clotted cream and strawberry jam alongside a pot of tea. Devon and Cornwall both claim it and argue over whether cream or jam goes on first.
how_to_eat: Split the scone; in Devon spread cream then jam, in Cornwall jam then cream.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'cream tea' at a tearoom.

name: Stargazy Pie
description: A Cornish pie of baked pilchards (sardines) with eggs and potato under a pastry crust, with the fish heads poking out to 'gaze at the stars'. It is tied to the village of Mousehole and Tom Bawcock's Eve on 23 December.
how_to_order: Look for it in Mousehole around Tom Bawcock's Eve; it is rarely on everyday menus.

name: Saffron Bun
description: A rich, spiced yeast bun flavoured and coloured with saffron and studded with currants and sultanas. In Cornwall it is also known as a tea treat bun or revel bun, baked for special occasions.
how_to_eat: Eat split and buttered with tea.
how_to_order: Buy from Cornish bakeries.

name: Scrumpy
description: Rough, often cloudy cider made locally by traditional methods, usually stronger than commercial ciders. It originates in the West Country.
how_to_eat: Drink cool by the pint, carefully, as it is often strong.
how_to_order: Ask for local scrumpy at West Country pubs or farm shops.

name: Yorkshire Pudding
description: A baked batter of eggs, flour and milk, poured into hot beef dripping, lard or other rendered fat. It was devised in Northern England to use the fat dripping from roasting meat and is part of the traditional Sunday roast.
how_to_eat: Eat filled with gravy, as a starter in Yorkshire or alongside roast beef.
how_to_order: Comes with a roast beef dinner; some pubs serve giant ones filled with stew.

name: Lancashire Hotpot
description: Lamb or mutton and onion topped with sliced potatoes and slowly baked in a lidded pot. It originated in Lancashire and was prized by the region's 19th-century cotton workers.
how_to_eat: Eat with pickled red cabbage.
how_to_order: Ask for hotpot at pubs in Lancashire.

name: Cumberland Sausage
description: A very long pork sausage of chopped meat, sold rolled in a coil and seasoned mainly with black and white pepper. 'Traditional Cumberland sausage' has Protected Geographical Indication status.
how_to_eat: Eat grilled as a whole coil with mash and onion gravy.
how_to_order: Look for it at Cumbrian butchers and pubs.

name: Eccles Cake
description: A small round turnover of flaky butter pastry filled with currants. It is named after the town of Eccles, now in Greater Manchester.
how_to_eat: Eat with tea; in Lancashire it is sometimes paired with a slice of Lancashire cheese.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries in the North West.

name: Parkin
description: A sticky gingerbread cake made with oatmeal and black treacle. It is traditionally eaten in Yorkshire and Lancashire around Bonfire Night (5 November).
how_to_order: Look for it at bakeries in autumn.

name: Stottie Cake
description: A round, flat white loaf from North East England, about 20 cm across. It is split and filled to make sandwiches, with fillings such as ham, bacon, sausage or pease pudding.
how_to_eat: Eat as a big sandwich.
how_to_order: Ask for a filled stottie at bakeries in North East England.

name: Scouse
description: A thick stew of lamb or beef with potatoes, carrots and onion. The dish gave Liverpool people their nickname, 'Scousers'.
how_to_eat: Eat with pickled red cabbage or beetroot and crusty bread.
how_to_order: Order it at cafés and pubs in Liverpool.

name: Melton Mowbray Pork Pie
description: A raised pie of chopped uncured pork in a hand-formed hot-water-crust pastry, with jellied pork stock inside. It has Protected Geographical Indication status for pies made in a zone around Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire.
how_to_eat: Eat cold, often with English mustard or pickle.
how_to_order: Buy from butchers and bakers in Melton Mowbray.

name: Bakewell Pudding
description: A Derbyshire dessert of flaky pastry with a layer of jam under a filling of egg and almond paste. It comes from the town of Bakewell and is different from the iced Bakewell tart.
how_to_eat: Eat warm with cream or custard.
how_to_order: Buy from the pudding shops in Bakewell.

name: Balti
description: A curry cooked quickly over high heat in vegetable oil and served in the thin steel bowl it is cooked in. It was developed in Birmingham in the 1970s, where the 'Balti Triangle' is known for its balti restaurants.
how_to_eat: Eat straight from the bowl using naan bread.
how_to_order: Order a chicken or lamb balti at a balti house in Birmingham.

name: Faggots and Peas
description: Meatballs of minced pork offal, such as heart and liver, with onion and breadcrumbs, wrapped in caul fat and baked. A traditional cheap dish, it is especially popular in the English Midlands and South Wales.
how_to_eat: Eat with mash and gravy.
how_to_order: Look for it at traditional pubs and cafés in the West Midlands.

name: Staffordshire Oatcake
description: A dense, savoury pancake made from oatmeal, flour and yeast, cooked on a griddle. It is a local speciality of north Staffordshire and the Potteries.
how_to_eat: Eat rolled around cheese, bacon or sausage.
how_to_order: Buy from oatcake shops in the Potteries.

name: Haggis
description: A savoury pudding of sheep's heart, liver and lungs minced with oatmeal, onion and spices. Often called Scotland's national dish, it is eaten at Burns Night suppers.
how_to_eat: Eat with 'neeps and tatties' (mashed swede and potato).
how_to_order: Order 'haggis, neeps and tatties' at Scottish pubs.

name: Cullen Skink
description: A thick soup of smoked haddock, potato and onion. It comes from the town of Cullen in Moray.
how_to_eat: Eat with crusty bread.
how_to_order: Look for it on pub and restaurant menus as a starter.

name: Arbroath Smokie
description: Haddock salted, dried in pairs and smoked over a hardwood fire. It is a speciality of Arbroath in Angus, and 'Arbroath smokies' has Protected Geographical Indication status.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, pulled off the bone.
how_to_order: Buy from smokehouses in Arbroath.

name: Scotch Pie
description: A small meat pie of hot-water-crust pastry, traditionally filled with minced mutton but now generally beef. It is a classic hot snack at football grounds.
how_to_eat: Eat hot by hand.
how_to_order: Buy from bakers or at football grounds.

name: Stornoway Black Pudding
description: Black pudding of beef suet, oatmeal, onion and animal blood made in the Western Isles. It has Protected Geographical Indication status.
how_to_eat: Eat sliced and fried, often in a cooked breakfast.
how_to_order: Look for it on breakfast menus.

name: Cranachan
description: A dessert of whipped cream, toasted oats, whisky, honey and raspberries. It began as a harvest celebration dish.
how_to_order: Look for it on Scottish dessert menus in summer.

name: Shortbread
description: A crumbly, unleavened biscuit made from sugar, butter and wheat flour. It is a traditional Scottish bake associated with Christmas and Hogmanay.
how_to_eat: Eat with tea.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries or gift shops.

name: Scotch Whisky
description: Malt or grain whisky made in Scotland and aged in oak casks for at least three years. 'Scotch whisky' is a protected geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Sip neat or with a few drops of water.
how_to_order: Ask for a single malt at a bar or tour a distillery.

name: Cawl
description: A broth of meat, usually lamb or beef, with leeks, potatoes and other vegetables. It is regarded as the national dish of Wales.
how_to_eat: Eat with bread and cheese.
how_to_order: Look for it in Welsh pubs, especially in winter.

name: Welsh Rarebit
description: Hot cheese sauce, often with ale, mustard or Worcestershire sauce, served on toast. Despite the name, there is no strong evidence that it originated in Wales.
how_to_eat: Eat hot.
how_to_order: Look for it on café lunch menus.

name: Laverbread
description: A purée of laver seaweed (Porphyra umbilicalis), boiled for several hours until soft and dark. 'Welsh laverbread' has Protected Designation of Origin status.
how_to_eat: Eat fried with bacon and cockles for breakfast.
how_to_order: Buy from markets in South Wales.

name: Welsh Cakes
description: Small, round, spiced cakes with dried fruit, traditionally cooked on a bakestone. They are a teatime staple across Wales.
how_to_eat: Eat warm dusted with sugar.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries and markets.

name: Bara Brith
description: A traditional Welsh tea bread flavoured with tea, dried fruits and spices; the name means 'speckled bread'. It was traditionally made by adding fruit, sugar and spices to bread dough.
how_to_eat: Eat sliced and buttered.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries and tearooms.

name: Glamorgan Sausage
description: A meatless sausage of cheese (usually Caerphilly) and leek or spring onion coated in breadcrumbs. It is a traditional Welsh vegetarian dish.
how_to_eat: Eat fried with chutney.
how_to_order: Look for it on Welsh menus.

name: Ulster Fry
description: Northern Ireland's cooked breakfast with bacon, sausages, egg, tomato and mushrooms, fried with soda farls and potato bread. The griddle breads set it apart from other full breakfasts.
how_to_eat: Eat as a big breakfast.
how_to_order: Ask for an 'Ulster fry' at cafés.

name: Soda Farl
description: A quadrant of soda bread, made by cooking a round of dough on a griddle and cutting it into four. Soda farls are a traditional part of the Ulster fry.
how_to_eat: Eat with butter and jam or fried.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries.

name: Potato Bread
description: A griddle bread in which potato replaces part of the wheat flour, often cut into farls. Traditionally it is part of the Ulster fry.
how_to_eat: Eat fried.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries or supermarkets.

name: Champ
description: Mashed potatoes combined with chopped spring onions, butter and milk. It is popular in Ulster, where it is served in a bowl with butter in a hollow in the centre.
how_to_eat: Eat with butter in the centre.
how_to_order: Look for it as a side in pubs.

name: Yellowman
description: A chewy, toffee-textured confectionery made from golden syrup and sugar, made bubbly with baking soda. It is particularly associated with the Ould Lammas Fair in Ballycastle, County Antrim.
how_to_eat: Eat broken into chunks.
how_to_order: Buy at fairs and sweet shops.

name: Irish Whiskey
description: Whiskey distilled on the island of Ireland, including at Bushmills in County Antrim. 'Irish whiskey' is a protected geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Sip neat or with water.
how_to_order: Ask for a Northern Irish whiskey at a pub.
